title: Dementia drugs: acetylcholine and glutamate
ariaLabel: Schematic of two signals in dementia: loss of cholinergic neurons lowers acetylcholine, and excess glutamate acting on NMDA receptors damages neurons. Donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine block acetylcholinesterase so acetylcholine lasts longer, and memantine blocks the NMDA receptor channel.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Acetylcholine
nodes.info: Acetylcholine from cholinergic neurons, which fall in number in Alzheimer disease.

nodes.label: Cholinergic signal
nodes.info: Acetylcholine signal for memory and attention.

nodes.label: Glutamate
nodes.info: Glutamate acting on NMDA receptors; too much causes calcium entry and neuron damage.

nodes.label: Excess excitation
nodes.info: Calcium overload and damage from over-active NMDA receptors.

nodes.label: Cognitive signalling
nodes.info: A teaching score for signalling that supports cognition. It does not show that any drug changes the course of the disease.

edges.label: AChE
edges.info: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) block acetylcholinesterase so acetylcholine lasts longer in the synapse.

edges.label: NMDA channel
edges.info: Memantine is an uncompetitive, low-affinity blocker of the NMDA receptor channel. It reduces excess activation while allowing normal signalling.

sources: Where each class acts. Cholinesterase inhibitors raise acetylcholine and memantine blocks the NMDA receptor channel. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Disease-modifying antibodies, other dementias and their drugs, antipsychotic cautions, benefit size and stopping, adverse effects (bradycardia, GI effects) and monitoring are left out. Cognitive signalling is drawn as a teaching score and does not claim a cure or slowing of disease. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
